answers.children: Yes — Golden Retrievers are good with children because of their patient, kind nature and gentle tolerance bred from their role retrieving waterfowl without damage. Their loyal and affectionate temperament leads them to nudge toddlers softly rather than knock them over despite large size and energetic playfulness. The breed's intelligence also helps them read family moods. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 9/10)
answers.other-pets: Yes — Golden Retrievers get along with other pets thanks to their sociable and gentle temperament developed alongside humans as gundogs in Scotland. They lack strong prey drive and show no same-sex tension, instead displaying friendly interest that extends to living harmoniously with cats or dogs when properly introduced.
answers.exercise: Golden Retrievers need at least one hour of exercise daily because they were originally bred in Scotland for retrieving waterfowl over long distances and rough terrain all day. Without it they become bored and destructive, shredding items or digging. Swimming, fetch and long walks suit their water-repelling coat and stamina.
answers.shedding: Yes — Golden Retrievers shed heavily with a medium double coat that drops fur year-round and worse seasonally. The dense undercoat and longer feathering on legs and tail trap loose hair that spreads through the house and clings to furniture, making cleanliness a challenge for owners.
answers.hypoallergenic: Golden Retrievers shed prodigiously from a dense double coat built for retrieving in cold water, and the feathering traps dander until it is brushed out. No breed is genuinely hypoallergenic, but this one sits at the opposite end of the range from the breeds usually suggested to allergy sufferers.
answers.training: Yes — Golden Retrievers are easy to train because of their high intelligence, eagerness to please and strong biddability rooted in their development as cooperative Scottish gundogs. They pick up commands quickly and excel in roles such as therapy and service work when given clear direction.
answers.lifespan: Golden Retrievers live 10-12 years. Their health robustness is challenged by a build and genetics that make them prone to issues affecting longevity, though their sturdy sporting frame from Scottish waterfowl retrieving origins supports active years when needs are met.
answers.size: Golden Retrievers reach 55-75 lb and stand 21-24 in at the shoulder as adults. Their substantial yet proportional build from selective breeding for stamina feels solid and comforting in the home, with enough presence to lean affectionately without being overwhelming for most families.
answers.barking: No — Golden Retrievers do not bark a lot because their original purpose as steady Scottish retrievers emphasised quiet work rather than alerting. They remain generally quiet, using their voice sparingly and without the frequent vocalisation seen in breeds developed for guarding or herding.
answers.apartment: No — Golden Retrievers do not suit apartment living because their energetic nature from waterfowl retrieving requires more than limited indoor space to prevent boredom and destruction. Their heavy shedding and need for daily activity also make settling indoors difficult without ample outlets.
answers.first-time: No — Golden Retrievers are not ideal as a first dog because their heavy shedding, high exercise demands from Scottish gundog heritage and emotional need for constant companionship challenge novices. Their intelligence makes training straightforward but the overall commitment to coat care and activity can overwhelm beginners.
